vignette:
She is eighty now, a widowed Middle Eastern woman who still introduces herself first through her work. Even in retirement, she thinks of herself as a social worker before anything else. For decades she has been the person who knows how to sit beside fear, how to make tea for grieving families, how to ask practical questions when other people freeze. What unsettles her most is that when the danger came to her own home, all of that training disappeared.

She speaks first about her son as a boy, before the illness, as if she needs to restore him to health before she can bear to describe what happened. He is lively, stubborn, always hungry, always running ahead of her in the market. Then, in one season, he becomes pale and exhausted. At first she explains it away the way many working mothers do. He is growing. He is studying too hard. It is a virus. She remembers feeling irritated with herself for worrying. She had spent years telling anxious parents not to jump to the worst conclusion. Then one evening he develops a fever that does not break, and she notices the frightening stillness in him. She says that was the first moment her body knew something was terribly wrong, even before the doctors spoke.

The hospitalization unfolds in her memory with unnatural clarity. She can describe the smell of antiseptic in the hallway, the scrape of a metal chair she drags to his bedside, the way fluorescent lights flatten everyone's face. When physicians begin speaking in grave, careful sentences, she latches onto tiny details instead of the meaning: the folded cuff of a white coat, a pen tapping a chart, a nurse avoiding her eyes. She understands only one thing-that her child may die. She says that from then on, time stops moving normally. Nights in the hospital feel endless; years later, whole months of her life around that period are missing.

She stays at the hospital as if vigilance itself might keep him alive. She memorizes medication schedules, watches monitors, argues with staff when they are late, and feels a piercing guilt whenever she leaves the room to wash or eat. If he sleeps too long, she jolts him awake to hear his voice. If a machine beeps, her heart hammers so hard she feels she might faint. She prays constantly, bargaining in whispers. When relatives tell her to rest, she hears it as a threat, as if stepping away would be the moment everything collapses.

Her son survives, but she says survival is not the same as the danger ending. Even after he comes home, she remains braced for catastrophe. A cough sends her into panic. If he closes his bedroom door, she imagines finding him unconscious. She begins checking on him repeatedly through the night, placing her hand near his face to feel his breathing. By day she returns to social work, sitting with clients in crisis while privately scanning her phone for missed calls. She becomes excellent at appearing calm. Coworkers praise her steadiness, not seeing that she is holding herself together by force.

Over the years, the fear changes shape rather than fading. She avoids driving near the hospital where he was treated because the building alone makes her palms sweat. Certain sounds still pull her backward-the rapid alarm of a monitor on television, the squeak of hospital shoes on polished floors, even the chemical smell of disinfectant. In those moments she is no longer an experienced professional or an elderly woman; she is again a mother in a hard chair waiting for someone to tell her whether her child will live. She sees flashes of his face during the worst nights, his skin too hot, his eyes half-open, and the images come without invitation. She tries to push them away, then feels ashamed that she cannot control her own mind.

Since her husband's death, the old fear has grown louder. She says widowhood has stripped away the last witness to that time. When she wakes from dreams in which she is running down a hospital corridor and never reaches the room, there is no one beside her to say, "It's over." She sleeps lightly, often getting up to check whether her adult son has texted, though he has his own family now and lives independently. If he does not answer quickly, she feels anger rise before reason can catch up. She knows she is treating a grown man like a fragile child, and this knowledge pains her.

She is embarrassed by how much of her life is organized around not feeling afraid. She changes the channel when medical dramas come on. She does not attend former colleagues' retirement gatherings if they are held at the hospital conference center. She keeps busy with community work, cooking, and helping neighbors navigate social services, but still feels a private fragility that surprises her. She has spent a lifetime being competent in emergencies for other people. What she carries now is the memory of learning that competence offers no protection when the person on the bed is your own child. Even in the present, with her son alive and her hair white and her working years behind her, some part of her remains in that hospital room, listening for the next alarm.
